name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5, sold as Syn-Coll, is a lab-made peptide attached to a fatty acid and added to anti-wrinkle and skin-firming creams, serums and microneedle patches. People use it for firmer, denser-looking skin and fewer wrinkles.

Suppliers describe it as a signal peptide that stimulates collagen synthesis through a TGF-beta-related pathway, with the fatty chain helping it cross the outer skin layer; this is mainly manufacturer description. Published studies have tested it in multi-ingredient products, such as hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with several peptides, and no standalone placebo-controlled trial was found.

paras: It is used as a leave-on serum or cream, or in microneedle patches, often combined with other peptides and hydrating ingredients. Firmness and wrinkle changes are typically assessed over several weeks of daily use.
No specific safety problems are documented in the sources found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5 (Syn-Coll) is a collagen-signalling peptide used in creams, serums and microneedle patches for firmer skin and fewer wrinkles. It prompts skin cells to make collagen, which densifies the dermis. Published studies are small and use multi-ingredient products.

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5, sold under the trade name Syn-Coll, is a synthetic lipopeptide used as an ingredient in anti-wrinkle and skin-firming cosmetics. It is marketed as a "signal peptide" intended to prompt skin cells to make more collagen, and it appears in creams, serums and microneedle patches.

Published material on the ingredient is sparse. A clinical study of hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with several bioactive peptides evaluated tolerability and skin effects of a multi-peptide product [1], and laboratory work has used it as a component of collagen nanoparticle formulations [2]. No published trial appears to isolate palmitoyl tripeptide-5 as a single active against placebo.

paras: The peptide is used in cosmetic products aimed at fine lines and loss of firmness. Manufacturers describe it as stimulating collagen production through a growth-factor-related signalling pathway (marketed as TGF-beta stimulation); these mechanism statements originate largely from supplier material rather than independent trials.

A monocentric clinical study examined hyaluronic acid microneedle patches loaded with a combination of bioactive peptides in ageing skin, assessing dermal tolerability and effects on skin parameters [1]. Because the patch contained several actives and used a microneedle delivery system, the results cannot be attributed to palmitoyl tripeptide-5 alone. A 2025 laboratory study combined lactoferrin, recombinant human collagen and palmitoyl tripeptide-5 in nanoparticles and reported anti-wrinkle, moisturising and whitening effects in experimental models [2]. A registered trial of Hydrafacial treatments listed skin quality and hydration outcomes in 27 adults [3]; the registration does not by itself show a specific effect of this peptide.
No specific adverse-effect literature for the peptide was identified. General reviews of cosmetic peptides discuss their use in formulations for sensitive skin [4].
